title: An output format argument with no default causes rmarkdown:::default_output_format to fail with cryptic error message.
description:
I ran into this developing a custom output format that worked fine from the console, but threw an error only when using the ‘knit’ button in RStudio.

Upon clicking the button I see this in the console:

    Error in merge_lists(as.list(formals(format_function)), format$options,  : 
      argument "base" is missing, with no default

I found the [cause here](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/main/R/output_format.R#L406) in `default_output_format()`

As you can see [here](https://github.com/MilesMcBain/issuecreep/blob/57cf4b25884f33d0953f1744aa76090bbd7112f9/R/github_issue.R#L27) the `repo` arg of my `github_issue` format had no default value.

So we get:

``` r
fake_output_format <- function(repo, number = NULL, action = "create") {
  NULL
}

fake_overlay <- list(repo = "milesmcabin/issuecreep", number = 1)

rmarkdown:::merge_lists(as.list(formals(fake_output_format)),
                        fake_overlay,
                        recursive = FALSE)
#> Error in rmarkdown:::merge_lists(as.list(formals(fake_output_format)), : argument "base" is missing, with no default

# And this is because in merge_lists:

base_list <- as.list(formals(fake_output_format))
base <- base_list[["repo"]]
is.list(base)
#> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos): argument "base" is missing, with no default

# because base is 'missing'
base
#> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos): argument "base" is missing, with no default
```

<sup>Created on 2022-09-02 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I think if I add a default to my output format all should be well. This was just a little hard to figure out and I didn’t find it documented anywhere, my apologies if this is so.

Maybe this case could be detected an some kind of more useful error thrown?

PS I drafted this and submitted this issue in RStudio with my `github_issue` format. An amazing job has been done with how extensible rmarkdown output formats are! :smile:

title: Consider adding "gt" as an available `df_print` option
description: `gt::gt()` has and will have many accessibility benefits as opposed to other `df_print` methods, such as `knitr::kable()`, etc. Although it's possible to customize `knitr::knit_print.data.frame` s3 method, it would be more convenient for users to have an option to choose `gt` for their `df_print` method. Additional benefit is that `gt` can be used for html, latex, word, and rtf, altogether.

title: References `\ref{fig:chunk_label}` in markdown with `pdf_document` output are only resolved when specifying chunk options in addition to `fig.cap`
description:
Consider the following example markdown:

````
---
title: MWE for figure labels
output:
  pdf_document:
    keep_md: true
    fig_height: 2
---

I think his reference should be resolved to the following Figure \ref{fig:plot_1}.

```{r plot_1, fig.cap = "Plot 1"}
plot(0)
```

Generation of the reference is triggered e.g. by requesting centering in the chunk
options (Figure \ref{fig:plot_2}).

```{r plot_2, fig.cap = "Plot 2", fig.align = "center"}
plot(0)
```
````

Rendering with `rmarkdown::render()` shows that only the second reference is resolved:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3621037/180624421-6624f3e2-af97-44de-9e9e-ed090f755d1f.png)

The markdown generated for the plots is the following:

````
```r
plot(0)
```

![Plot 1](mwe_files/figure-latex/plot_1-1.pdf)
````

and

````
```r
plot(0)
```

\begin{figure}

{\centering \includegraphics{mwe_files/figure-latex/plot_2-1} 

}

\caption{Plot 2}\label{fig:plot_2}
\end{figure}
````
Reading the [documentation](https://yihui.org/knitr/options/#plots) of the plot specific chunk options, especially of `fig.lp`, I would expect that the label would also be generated for the first chunk.

title: [FR] Allow users to use the python version of Pandoc
description:
Hi folks, thanks in advance for all the help :)

We're currently using Pandoc on Databricks, which doesn't allow for users to run shell scripts and install Pandoc themselves with `apt-get`. There are ways that admins can run 'init_scripts' on a users behalf, but a much easier way would be for rmarkdown to accept the [pypi version of pandoc](https://pypi.org/project/pandoc/) (which normal users can install easily in Databricks without permissions).

To call the pypi version of pandoc, it's as simple as running `python -m pandoc [pandoc commands]` instead of straight `pandoc  [pandoc commands]`.

I'm digging into the code that I [think controls the calling of Pandoc from shell](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/main/R/pandoc.R), but it seems like 3 things need to happen:

- Amend sources in [find_pandoc()](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/main/R/pandoc.R#L641) to search in installed python3 packages
- Amend [set_pandoc_version()](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/main/R/pandoc.R#L695) to additionally return a 'command' that is used to call pandoc, that overrides the standard 'pandoc' with 'python -m pandoc'
- Ensure any functions that call pandoc use the new path from the amended `set_pandoc_version()`

I'm trying to unpick this myself but I'm also new to R, so the above could also be completely wrong.

Thanks again!

title: [FR] Add an Option Called lower-headers for github_document
description:
This is for GitHub documents.
Since the top-level header (`#`) is only used for the title, you have to use second-level headers after that (`##`).
This is inconvenient since I will always set the title using the `title` option in the YAML metadata.
I would like an option to automatically lower all the headers.
For example, `#` becomes `##`, `##` becomes `###`, etc.
You can add a file called `lower-headers.lua`:

```lua
function Header(el)
  el.level = el.level + 1
  return el
end
```

Then you simply just have to include it in `pandoc_args` via `--lua-filters`.
This feature is great because it doesn't mess with anything before the main body of the document.
So the title section will still be a top-level header.
It seems appropriate to make this option enabled by default too, since I see no reason not to use it.

title: [FR] Skipping heading hierarchy
description:
<!--

Welcome to the rmarkdown GitHub repo 👋

Thanks for taking the time to file a feature request! Please start by searching for an existing feature request to avoid creating duplicate requests. If you find an existing feature request, please give it a thumbs-up reaction, as we'll use these reactions to help prioritize the implementation of these features in the future.

If the feature has not yet been filed, follow these advice to write good feature request: 

- Provide a clear and concise description of the problem this proposed feature would address? For example, I struggle to do `[...]` with rmarkdown.

- Try to detail what you want to happen.

- Have you thought of alternative solutions or workarounds you've considered ? We'll be glad to know about them!

- Any other context or screenshots about your feature request that would help us understand ? Please include them!


If you'd also like to offer a solution, you are welcome to submit a pull request, although we appreciate filing an issue first to confirm that the team agrees with your idea and is happy with your basic proposal. Please read this guide for more information: <https://yihui.org/issue/#proposing-a-feature-implementation-or-bug-fix>

-->

WCAG2.1 expects the use of headings to follow as h1, h2, h3. Skipping from h1 to h3 would not be permitted. Likewise, headings should always contain content. These issues are present within the rmarkdown header, where the YAML title (h1) can be followed by author (not h2) etc. This is very confusing for screen reader users who rely on the heading hierarchy to efficiently navigate web pages to their desired content.

This gets a bit more complex as you consider table of contents, variable document YAML metadata (subtitle or no, author, date and so on). The approach in [`access_rmd::return_heading()`](https://github.com/datasciencecampus/accessrmd/blob/main/R/return_heading.R) is to return styled p tags for author / date etc. This is what we were advised was more 'semantically correct' during our accessibility audit.

If toc is specified, the most direct solution for us was to ensure toc_float was TRUE. The floating toc passed our accessibility checks, while the standard toc had additional accessibility issues (though I can't seem to find the reference in our docs, it would be best to check that within [WAVE](https://wave.webaim.org/) to help resolve).

**WCAG guidance**

1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A) 

Semantic markup is used to designate headings (`<h1>`), regions/landmarks, lists (`<ul>`, `<ol>`, and `<dl>`), emphasized or special text (`<strong>`, `<code>`, `<abbr>`, `<blockquote>`, for example), etc. Semantic markup is used appropriately. 

2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A) 

2.4.6 Headings and Labels (Level AA) 

Page headings and labels for form and interactive controls are informative. Avoid duplicating heading (e.g., "More Details") or label text (e.g., "First Name") unless the structure provides adequate differentiation between them.

title: [FR] Consistent image alt text render
description:
<!--

Welcome to the rmarkdown GitHub repo 👋

Thanks for taking the time to file a feature request! Please start by searching for an existing feature request to avoid creating duplicate requests. If you find an existing feature request, please give it a thumbs-up reaction, as we'll use these reactions to help prioritize the implementation of these features in the future.

If the feature has not yet been filed, follow these advice to write good feature request: 

- Provide a clear and concise description of the problem this proposed feature would address? For example, I struggle to do `[...]` with rmarkdown.

- Try to detail what you want to happen.

- Have you thought of alternative solutions or workarounds you've considered ? We'll be glad to know about them!

- Any other context or screenshots about your feature request that would help us understand ? Please include them!


If you'd also like to offer a solution, you are welcome to submit a pull request, although we appreciate filing an issue first to confirm that the team agrees with your idea and is happy with your basic proposal. Please read this guide for more information: <https://yihui.org/issue/#proposing-a-feature-implementation-or-bug-fix>

-->

Accessibility audit pointed to unreliable rendering of image alt text when using markdown syntax in Rmd documents knitted to html. At times, the markdown syntax renders correctly - image with non-visible alt text available to screen readers. On occasion, the image renders with visible alt text. Screen readers would then read the alt text twice as the visible and non-visible alt text tags. This is an accessibility error and results in navigation issues with screen reader users tabbing through the page tags. 

Also, no alt text is included with charts as standard.

The [approach taken in `accessrmd::access_img()` ](https://github.com/datasciencecampus/accessrmd/blob/main/R/access_img.R) is only compatible with `ggplot2` charts and images on disk. That is to say, base plot compatibility has not yet been achieved. But the idea is to write ggplot charts to tempfile, then read as if it were any other disk image, embedding the filepath within a html img tag. 

The html img tag approach passed our accessibility audit, we just found that most of our colleagues favoured the less reliable markdown syntax and needed a faster way for them to write code that would pass our service standard.

A good website for checking these issues is [WAVE webaim](https://wave.webaim.org/). You can also use the chrome WAVE plugin. Opening your rendered html docs within the WAVE interface is a good first start for troubleshooting many of the WCAG2.1 'gotchas'.

Documents rendered with inappropriate alt text for images and charts result in accessibility issues for screen reader users. The [approach taken with `accessrmd`](https://github.com/datasciencecampus/accessrmd/blob/main/R/sus_alt.R). It could be best to raise warnings on knit if any image alt text were equal to the following:

- [ ] no alt attribute value
- [ ] 'nbsp'
- [ ] 'spacer'
- [ ]  alt attribute is the same as src attribute value

Additionally, English, German & Korean language values have associated character limits for alt text. Please [see the `accessrmd` implementation](https://github.com/datasciencecampus/accessrmd/blob/main/R/find_alt_lim.R).

title: [FR] Use `--wrap=preserve` by default
description:
Recent pandoc versions automatically wrap long lines and this has caused some issues in some formats([bookdown](https://github.com/rstudio/bookdown/issues/504), [distill](https://github.com/rstudio/distill/issues/463), [rticles](https://github.com/rstudio/rticles/issues/490)).

I am trying to create a tutorial on how to automate R report generation and have created a contained project at https://github.com/erikaduan/abs_labour_force_report.

When I render this report template directly, the [github document](https://github.com/erikaduan/abs_labour_force_report/blob/main/code/02_create_report_template.md) contains the correct relative figure path to display my ggplot graph.

## Bug Report

I am filing this issue because I am observing circumstances where `error=TRUE` is not honored in code chunks. When the chunk contains `ggplot2` code _and_ the error is related to an incorrect `aes()` specification, it seems that rmarkdown is expecting to include an output image associated with that chunk. There should not be any image, because `error=TRUE`. Other errors in `ggplot2` code that are not related to incorrectly specified `aes()` arguments do not have this problem - `error=TRUE` is honored and the document knits. Similarly, base R `graphics` plots with errors do not prevent knitting. 

I have included here an Rmarkdown file and its rendered HTML with several chunks that demonstrate what I am seeing. I have commented out the chunks that prevent knitting in spite of `error=TRUE`. When I uncomment these chunks, the document does not render with errors that I include in the comments within.
[potential_bug.zip](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/files/8767001/potential_bug.zip)
Note that I originally observed this with `rmarkdown 2.14`, so I installed `2.14.1` and the problem remained (hence it's in the `sessionInfo()` in the rendered HTML.)

The Rmarkdown itself contains a `sessionInfo()` chunk relevant to what is in the environment during knitting, but either way I am also pasting my `sessionInfo()` from Console below:

title: [FR] improve default syntax highlighting for vignettes
description: When a vignette is rendered, any embedded code is also highlighted. However, it seems like the default highlighter is a bit limited in a few ways: - Brackets (e.g. `(` and `)`) are not tokenized, and so they cannot be styled; - Arguments names (and a following `=`) are tokenized as a single token, and so cannot be styled independently. (https://invent.kde.org/frameworks/syntax-highlighting/-/blob/master/data/syntax/r.xml#L58) - `:=` is not tokenized as a single operator; in particular, the `=` following a `:` is tokenized as an error. *(please ignore the class names here; those are RStudio-specific experiments)* My understanding is that this highlighting / tokenization is performed by pandoc, with some extra highlight rules provided here: https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/de02c926371fdadc4d92f08e1ad7b77db069be49/inst/rmarkdown/templates/html_vignette/resources/vignette.css#L187-L202 Could this be changed / improved by changing the highlight engine used by pandoc for vignettes?

title: pandoc_available() function crashes on rhub "macos-m1-bigsur-release"
description:
When running `rhub::check(platform="macos-m1-bigsur-release")` on a package that has an R Markdown vignette, the package check fails with a subscript out of bounds error.  This appears to be a problem on rhub that rmarkdown is not protecting itself against.

Here's a copy of a post about it I just made to the R-package-devel mailing list:

I've localized the issue.  In the function 
rmarkdown:::get_pandoc_version (here: 
https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/84dfc6674083f355d4f8c87dca8d85f85ca53bad/R/pandoc.R#L676-L693), 
they think they know a path to pandoc, and run "pandoc --version" to get 
the version number.  It appears they get a zero length result, so line 
683 gets the subscript out of bounds error and everything dies.


To reproduce, create a test package which imports rmarkdown and has this 
single line of R code:

     available <- rmarkdown::pandoc_available()

then submit that package to rhub using

     rhub::check(platform="macos-m1-bigsur-release")

It will fail with a message like this:

  248#> * installing *source* package ‘testpkg3’ ...

  249#> ** using staged installation

  250#> ** R

  251#> ** byte-compile and prepare package for lazy loading

  252#> Error in strsplit(info, "\n")[[1]] : subscript out of bounds

  253#> Error: unable to load R code in package ‘testpkg3’

  254#> Execution halted

  255#> ERROR: lazy loading failed for package ‘testpkg3’

  256#> * removing 
‘/Users/userDqIwNAjs/Rtemp/Rtmp6N8Dtr/Rinst146057d7e12c1/testpkg3’

==========================================================

I discovered that section headers with consecutive underscores (_) could mess up section settings (wrapped in {} after the header) in HTML output.

For example, if I want to remove numbering of some sections with `{.unnumbered}` and prevent them from appearing in ToC with `{.unlisted}`, headers with two or more consecutive underscores will not let such settings take effect.

A minimal reprex:

````
---
title: "Untitled"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_float: true
    number_sections: true
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

# R Markdown

Let us see how consecutive underscores (_) affect header options:

## Subsetction 1 {.unlisted .unnumbered}

foo

## Subsection_2 {.unlisted .unnumbered}

bar

## Subsection__3 {.unlisted .unnumbered}

baz

## Subsection___4 {.unlisted .unnumbered}

uhh

````

This will knit into an HTML page like this:

```
Untitled
1 R Markdown
Let us see how consecutive underscores (_) affect header options:

Subsetction 1
foo

Subsection_2
bar

1.1 Subsection__3 {.unlisted .unnumbered}
baz

1.2 Subsection___4 {.unlisted .unnumbered}
uhh
```

We can see that section settings are not taking effect on "Subsection__3" and "Subsection___4".

title: [FR] Add a new type of dependency that bundles lua filter and other type of dependencies
description:
We are more more adding feature based on Lua filters, and they often require to have other dependencies added like CSS or JS, but it could even be LaTeX dependencies. 

Currently, we need to do that by creating dependencies in several object and then adding them at the right place in the output format. 

I have a secret wish to  a way to have a _feature extensions bundle_ where we have a  `htmlDependency()` with a Lua filter requirements. Something that we could write in a wrapped way, and that **rmarkdown** could unwrapped and use the correct way. We don't have a `lua_dependency` component, and maybe that would make sense to have at some point adding more feature like this 
````r
lua_dependency(
	filters = "code-folding-lua",
    html_deps = htmlDependency(
    	"codefolding-lua",
	    version = "1.1",
    	src = pkg_file("rmd/h/navigation-1.1"),
	    stylesheet = "codefolding-lua.css",
    	all_files = FALSE
  )
}
````

We could then group some features. 

It could also be more generic like an `rmd_dependency()` (suggestion of @atusy) and could indeed probably be interesting if we considered it would bundle everything

```r
rmd_dependency(
  filters = # lua filters
  html_deps = # htmlDepedency()
  latex_deps = # latex_dependencies()
)
```

This way a feature could be grouped with all its component. This could also be extended to knitr to support having a lua filter as part of dependencies to add, working the same as with HTML deps or LaTeX deps with `knitr::knit_meta()`

It would not help make things works better, but I feel it would makes this cleaner, the same way JS and CSS are grouped for an HTML deps.

_Originally posted by @cderv in https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/pull/2340#discussion_r841559258_

```
I confirm that I've tried the development versions of rmarrdown and knitr.

This issue first occurred after updating all of my packages today, in particular rmarkdown. I've also updated RStudio. I believe that I've gone from version 2.12 of rmarkdown to 2.13.3.

Here's is the markdown that produces an error.
````
---
title: "Frustration: One Year With R"
author: "Reece Goding"
output:
  github_document:
    toc: true
    number_sections: true
---
```{r, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE)
```
### Mapply Challenge
Maybe you think I'm clutching at straws? I admit, I do sometimes wonder if my outrage is unjustified. Let's settle this with a challenge. If you win, then by all means close this document and write me off as a madman. If you lose, then maybe I've got a point. Okay, here's your challenge:

---  
**CHALLENGE**

Taking in to account R's vector recycling rules, figure out how `mapply()`'s `MoreArgs` and `...` arguments differ and when you would want to pass something as a `MoreArgs` argument rather than in the `...` argument. No cheating by going online (trust me, it won't help much anyway). Solve this without leaving your R IDE. You're encouraged to check the documentation.
---
If my criticisms are true, you will find that `mapply()`'s documentation is of little help and that your confidence in your R knowledge is too small to make an educated guess.

---
**HINT 1**

Don't try to cheat by looking at `mapply()`'s code; Most of it is in C and therefore will be of no help to you.
---
---
**HINT 2**

You might think that the documentation for `sapply()` will help you, but it'll actually mislead you because `mapply()`'s `...` is essentially `sapply()`'s `X` and `sapply()`'s `...` is most like `mapply()`'s `MoreArgs`.
---

Solution below. Time to stop scrolling.

---
**SOLUTION**

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

**How do `MoreArgs` and `...` differ?**
  
  It's tough to explain. `mapply()` uses the default vector recycling rules for the `...` arguments but reuses every element of `MoreArgs` for each call. Because the `MoreArgs` argument must be a list and R recycles the elements of lists (e.g. using a length 1 list as a `...` argument will have the element of that list reused for each call), the difference is subtle to the point of near invisibility. Ultimately, `MoreArgs = list(a, b, c)` is equivalent to using `list(a)`, `list(b)`, and `list(c)` as three separate `...` arguments. The answer is therefore that `MoreArgs` only exists as syntactic sugar for this `...` case.
  
**When use `MoreArgs` rather than `...`?**
  
  Beyond what I've already said, I barely have any idea. If you want to keep some function arguments fixed for each call, then just use an anonymous function. I struggle to invent a useful example of where I'd even consider using `MoreArgs`, never mind one that doesn't look tailor-made to make the anonymous function option look better. The one and only example that the documentation gives for using `MoreArgs` does not help here. Their example of `mapply(rep, times = 1:4, MoreArgs = list(x = 42))` is identical to `mapply(rep, times = 1:4, list(x = 42))`. Read that again: **You can get identical functionality by deleting the thing that they're trying to demonstrate!**

**Bonus**
  
  Did you notice that the documentation for `mapply()` has a notable omission? It doesn't mention this, but you can call `mapply()` without the `...` argument, e.g. `mapply(rep, MoreArgs = list(1:4))`. You won't get sensible output, but you also don't get any warnings or errors.
---

If I've won this challenge, then allow me to take a victory lap by making the following point: By giving you the options of using `...`, `MoreArgs`, or an anonymous function to do the same task, R gives you plenty of room to confuse yourself without providing any help in its documentation. Either provide fewer options, document them better, or make them so commonplace and consistent within the language that I only need to understand it once in order to understand it everywhere!
````
The error is:
```
YAML parse exception at line 1, column 1,
while scanning an alias:
did not find expected alphabetic or numeric character
Error: pandoc document conversion failed with error 64
Execution halted
```

To fix this, deleting all of my `---` lines seems sufficient, but I can't fathom why. Did version 2.1.3 change anything to do with these? I'm confident that this all worked without issue on version 2.1.2.

title: _output.yml overrides output format in frontmatter
description:
Hello.

First:
- I hope that this has not already be mentioned, I looked for it but did not find anything.
- I am wondering if this is really an issue or an intended behavior that is not so clear in the documentation.

When using rmardown::render on a input file located in a directory where an _output.yml file exists, I have this behavior:
- the output format is taken first from _output.yaml (and only from this file without no other option to render)
- and then from what is defined in the frontmatter part of the input file.

As already said, I may have missed something in the documentation, but I was expecting exactly the inverse behavior... as I used _output.yml as a "default" configuration for rmardown::render when no frontmatter is defined in a file.

This can be seen with this input file (let's say its name is "presentation.Rmd")
````
---
title: "Test"

    beamer_presentation:
        slide_level: 1
lang: en
---

````

bookdown::pdf_book:
  toc: true
---

output_format_yaml)

that I would change in

output_format_yaml <- merge_output_options(output_format_yaml,
common_output_format_yaml)

title: Long title in ioslides_presentation breaks knitted html
description:
### Short description
When generating a new R markdown presentation (HTML (ioslides)) from RStudio using a long title, the knitted result that is shown is just a black window.

### Versions
pandoc: 1.7+
rmarkdown: 2.12.2

### MWE

Knit the file test.Rmd containing:
```rmarkdown
---
title: "This is a very long title that breaks rmarkdown or knitr or something"
output: 
    ioslides_presentation
---
```
result:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4580455/157273704-7ff52979-f0ec-4ba9-8cc2-da2becdd58e6.png)

### workaround:
```rmarkdown
---
title: "This is a very long title that breaks rmarkdown or knitr or something"
output: 
    ioslides_presentation:
      pandoc_args: [
        "--wrap", "none"
      ]
---
```
result:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4580455/157273897-3566f09c-c501-4243-8df5-aed0d104d0ed.png)

### Generated html
The new line in the title in the javascript section is causing this issue:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <title>This is a very long title that breaks rmarkdown or knitr or something</title>

  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="chrome=1">
  <meta name="generator" content="pandoc" />




  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes">

  <base target="_blank">

  <script type="text/javascript">
    var SLIDE_CONFIG = {
      // Slide settings
      settings: {
                title: "This is a very long title that breaks rmarkdown
 or knitr or something",
                        useBuilds: true,
        usePrettify: true,
        enableSlideAreas: true,
        enableTouch: true,
                      },

      // Author information
      presenters: [
            ]
    };
  </script>

<!-- more stuff over here :-) -->

</html>
```

title: [FR] Animation in Microsoft word with rmarkdown
description:
<!--

I work on an open source project www.gwsdat.net with the University of Glasgow. It is an R package with Shiny front end to analyse groundwater data and used by students, environmental engineers and regulators. 

It would be fantastic to be able to embed  animations from the app into a word document. I know you can do this in HTML and pdf - but the trouble here is that the document is not easily editable. 

I've previously asked the question here: https://community.rstudio.com/t/animation-in-microsoft-word-with-rmarkdown/97616/2  but had no response. 

-->


I work on an open source project www.gwsdat.net with the University of Glasgow. It is an R package with Shiny front end to analyse groundwater data and used by students, environmental engineers and regulators. 

It would be fantastic to be able to embed  animations from the app into a word document. I know you can do this in HTML and pdf - but the trouble here is that the document is not easily editable. 

I've previously asked the question here: https://community.rstudio.com/t/animation-in-microsoft-word-with-rmarkdown/97616/2  but had no response.

title: [FR] Have equal spacing for nested lists
description:
For example, this is what my `example.Rmd` document looks like:

````md
---
title: "Plan"
output: 
    html_document:
      keep_md: true
---

- Day 1: do that but this way

  * step 1
  * step 2

- Day 2: do something else
````

The HTML output for this document doesn't have equal spacing between the top-level unordered list items and the child unordered list items:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11330453/156374610-40a539b4-aa08-4133-9455-3103c43606d5.png)

But if I convert the generated `.md` file to HTML using `pandoc`,

```bash
pandoc example.md -o example.html
```

I get the desired output:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11330453/156375166-c2d0f4ba-b6e7-4e23-b023-63585900fb5c.png)

Is it possible for `rmarkdown` to support this by default?

Thanks.

title: Apply lua filter after integration of latex template [FR]
description:
I am trying to use lua filters to move figure captions at the end of the document, in a section that exists only in the latex template I'm using, not in the markdown.

After some reading, I understood this is not doable at the moment since filters are applied before the integration of the markdown in the template.

The only hack I thought of was to reuse pandoc on the .tex produced by rmarkdown to produce a new final latex document:

`pandoc -f latex -t latex -o test2.tex --lua-filter=my_filters.lua test.tex`

but also this approach was not optimal since it drops all non-standard/non-structural elements (maybe because I didn't do it properly).

Is there a way to apply the filter after the integration of the markdown in the template? and if it is not possible, would make sense to add this feature?

DISCLOSURE: I raised the question also here https://stackoverflow.com/questions/71289289/rmarkdown-with-pandoc-templates-apply-lua-filter-on-intermediate-tex, because I was not sure this is something that is doable right now or could be instead a feature request.

Thanks

title: add \pdfoutput to preamble for arXiv sumbission
description:
Hello,

Seems strange this issue wasn't raised before since rmarkdown is much used for scientific publishing.

I recently submitted a manuscript to arXiv, but it failed because they need the option `\pdfoutput = 1` within the first 5 lines of the preamble when processing a .tex file.

Using the `in_header` option doesn't seem to work because if one is using a template (I am using rticles::arxiv_article()) then the latex code passed to `in_header` is appended much later in the document.

How does one add `\pdfoutput = 1` in rmarkdown forcing it to be at the top of the produced .tex document?

title: Allow `output_file` to be a function in `render()` [FR]
description:
<!--

Welcome to the rmarkdown GitHub repo 👋

Thanks for taking the time to file a feature request! Please start by searching for an existing feature request to avoid creating duplicate requests. If you find an existing feature request, please give it a thumbs-up reaction, as we'll use these reactions to help prioritize the implementation of these features in the future.

If the feature has not yet been filed, follow these advice to write good feature request: 

- Provide a clear and concise description of the problem this proposed feature would address? For example, I struggle to do `[...]` with rmarkdown.

- Try to detail what you want to happen.

- Have you thought of alternative solutions or workarounds you've considered ? We'll be glad to know about them!

- Any other context or screenshots about your feature request that would help us understand ? Please include them!


If you'd also like to offer a solution, you are welcome to submit a pull request, although we appreciate filing an issue first to confirm that the team agrees with your idea and is happy with your basic proposal. Please read this guide for more information: <https://yihui.org/issue/#proposing-a-feature-implementation-or-bug-fix>

-->

It would be useful to have an easy way to reuse metadata included in the YAML front matter of an RMarkdown file for generating output file names when rendering. This originally [came up on StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/q/71173343/4550695). 

At the moment it's simple enough to do with `yaml_front_matter()` if the metadata doesn't include R expressions. Just extract the metadata from the RMarkdown file, and build the output file name.

However, it becomes quite a bit more complicated if the metadata fields contain expressions that need to be rendered first. One way to do that is to keep the intermediate Markdown file, and extract the metadata from there. For example:

``` md
---
title: "Untitled"
author: "Jane Doe"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output: word_document
knit: >
  (function(input_file, encoding) {
    # Render, keeping intermediate files for extracting front matter
    md_dir <- tempdir()
    output_file_temp <- rmarkdown::render(
      input = input_file,
      output_file = tempfile(),
      intermediates_dir = md_dir,
      clean = FALSE
    )
    
    # Get the rendered front matter from the intermediate Markdown file
    md_file <- fs::path_ext_set(fs::path_file(input_file), ".knit.md")
    metadata <- rmarkdown::yaml_front_matter(fs::path(md_dir, md_file))
    
    # Build output file name based on rendered metadata
    output_name <- with(metadata, paste(title, "by", author, "on", date))
    output_ext <- fs::path_ext(output_file_temp)
    output_file <- fs::path_ext_set(output_name, output_ext)
    
    fs::file_move(output_file_temp, output_file)
  })
---

204 No Content
```

Would it be possible to allow the `output_file` argument to `render()` to be a function that gets the rendered metadata as an argument? The above could then become:

``` md
---
title: "Untitled"
author: "Jane Doe"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output: word_document
knit: >
  (function(input_file, encoding) {
    rmarkdown::render(
      input = input_file,
      output_file = function(metadata) {
        with(metadata, paste(title, "by", author, "on", date))
      }
    )
  })
---

204 No Content
```

And the resulting output file would be named `Untitled by Jane Doe on 2022-02-18.docx`.

description:
When I work with the tree package, I cannot access a part of its output from an Rmd document, but I can access it with the exact same code in the console. Please find an Rmd exemplifying the problem below and the HTML report with the session info attached.

output: html_document

Let's create some small data for a `tree::tree` approach:

```{r}
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
library(tree); set.seed(1)
summary(x <- data.frame(
   Y=factor(rep(letters[1:2], each=250)),

If

xfun::session_info()
```

title: header-includes in `beamer_presentation()` is not working as with `pdf_document()`
description:
If `beamer_presentation` is specified as output, macros with an optional argument at the end get incorrectly parsed to tex. Take for example the following example with `\setbeamertemplate{footline}[frame number]` in the header-includes:

```
---
title: "**TITLE**"
subtitle: "Subtitle"
author: "Name"
institute: ""
date: January 25, 2022
output:
  beamer_presentation:
    keep_tex: true
header-includes:
  - \setbeamertemplate{footline}[frame number]
---

test
```

The resulting .tex file will have 

```
\setbeamertemplate{footline}{[}frame number{]}
```

instead of

```
\setbeamertemplate{footline}[frame number]
```

If I change the output to something else, the macro will be parsed correctly:

```
---
title: "**TITLE**"
subtitle: "Subtitle"
author: "Name"
institute: ""
date: January 25, 2022
output:
  pdf_document:
    keep_tex: true
header-includes:
  - \usepackage{beamerarticle}
  - \setbeamertemplate{footline}[frame number]
---

test

title: Wrong post processing pipeline for pdf_document() conversion
description:
Found while working #2264, 

> The post processor will be run after on the output file being a pdf. Until recently, pdf_document() had no post processor and it seemed to work. But there is one today and I don't think it is working correctly. Oddly, it throws a warning only in debug mode.

A recent fix introduced a post processor in the `pdf_document()` output. https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/commit/5a3e941bbebf14c1a1a797125ffc414f61edc664

This creates some issues I believe but it does not show in CI oddly. 

`output_format$post_processor()` is supposed to run on the output of the Pandoc conversion. While looking into the other issue https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/issues/2264#issuecomment-999476710, it happens that the conversion step (before post processing) will generate a PDF file using `latexmk()`.  when output file is pdf for example.
https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/0af6b3556adf6e393b2da23c66c695724ea7bd2d/R/render.R#L974-L981

In that case the `post_processor()` will try to post process the PDF file 
https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/5a3e941bbebf14c1a1a797125ffc414f61edc664/R/pdf_document.R#L191-L200

This does not work obviously. Reprex: 

````r
dir.create(tmp_dir <- tempfile())
owd <- setwd(tmp_dir)
xfun::download_file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/main/tests/testthat/test-formats.Rmd")
rmarkdown::render("test-formats.Rmd", rmarkdown::pdf_document(), quiet = TRUE)
#> Warning message:
#> In readLines(con, warn = FALSE) :  invalid input found on input connection 'test-formats.pdf'
````

The post processing step should happen before `latexmk()` after Pandoc conversion from `.md` to `.tex`. I don't think it is working right now.

Or maybe the `latexmk()` rendering should happen in the `pdf_document()` post processing 🤔 But that would mean for user creating custom output that they need to use `pdf_document()` as base format or do the conversion themself. Maybe room for a `pdf_document_base()` format that does essential processing ? 

I get all those warning message when running tests locally, I am not sure why we don't see them in CI. 🤔

title: [FR] an overleaf for rmarkdown
description:
R markdown is a perfect drop-in replacement for LaTeX. However, in real life, we usually need to collaborate with other people, including people who don't use R markdown.

For LaTeX, there is an online editor [OverLeaf](https://www.overleaf.com/) (like google Docs for LaTeX), which allows collaborative writing online. They also have a mode similar to the R markdown visual mode, which allows collaboration even with WYSIWYG users.

For R Markdown, there is currently nothing like overleaf yet. The Rstudio online is close to it, but there are some core functions missing: change tracking and comment system. And also, the interface is too complex for the non-programmers.

I'm wondering if it is possible for Rstudio to hold an online platform, that is specific to R markdown editing, which allows seamless collaborative editing with both markdown user and WYSIWYG users.

An alternative strategy is to use [`redoc`](https://github.com/noamross/redoc/), which allows bi-directional conversations between Microsoft Word and R markdown. However, it is currently suspended and unstable.

Thank you so much!

title: Knitting HTML from RStudio versus using rmarkdown::render() treats iframes differently
description:
Hello, 

I am trying to embed standalone HTML files within a larger HTML report generated with Rmd using iframes. When I knit to HTML within RStudio, I get the expected behavior, which is an independent HTML file that can be shared with others. When I instead generate an HTML using `rmarkdown::render()` from the command line, the name of the iframe source file is included in the rendered HTML, and the iframes appear as broken links if the paths to the iframe source files are not maintained. 

Here is an example with this `minimal.html`:
```{html}
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>title</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    hello there
  </body>
</html>
```
and this `embed-iframes.Rmd`: 
````
---
title: "Embed iframes"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
data(cars)
```

```{r, results = "asis"}
# it needs to work inside a loop
for (i in 1){
  # print a plot
  plot(cars$speed, cars$dist)
  
  # print an iframe from an external html
  print(htmltools::tags$iframe(title = "My embedded document", src = "minimal.html"))
}
```
````

In the attached zip file, there are two HTMLs: 

* `embed-iframes.html`: This is the HTML when knitted within Rstudio and what I would also like to get from `rmarkdown::render()`.  "hello there" is visible in an iframe as expected. 

* `embed-iframes-RMDrender.html`: This is the HTML generated using `Rscript -e "rmarkdown::render('embed-iframes.Rmd', output_file='embed-iframes-RMDrender.html')"`. Instead of "hello there", you see a broken link icon with "It may have been moved, edited, or deleted" (as long as `minimal.html` is not in the same path as `embed-iframes-RMDrender.html`). The path to the iframe source file, i.e. "minimal.html", is written explicitly in the HTML code. 

My current workaround is to share folders with the HTML report and all iframe source HTMLs, but this is not ideal. I imagine there's a pandoc setting to get the iframe source embedded directly into the rendered HTML report, but I am at a bit of a loss. I would appreciate any help.

title: Incorrect direction of single curved quote if we use a citation followed by 's and a word followed by' in the same para
description:
If R Markdown has a citation followed by 's and another word followed by ' (but not by 's) then the single quote is in the wrong direction. Below is a MWE where @cat is a reference to Cat (2021).
```
1. Correct direction: cat's fur.
2. Correct direction: cat's fur. dogs' fur.
3. Correct direction: cat's fur. dog's fur.
4. Correct direction: @cat's fur. dog's fur.
5. Incorrect direction: @cat's fur. dogs' fur.
```
The output should be:
```
Cat (2021)'s fur. dogs' fur.
``` 
Instead we get:
```
Cat (2021)`s fur. dogs' fur.
``` 
Note the quote after Cat (2021) is a left quote and not a right quote.

dogs' fur only trips the code if there is a citation followed by a quote (case 5 in the MWE) but not if there is a word followed by 's (case 2 in the MWE). 

In cases 3 and 4, we have dog's fur. In those cases, the input does not trip up the parser.

title: [FR] Output format based on Pandoc "defaults file"
description:
This is a mixture between a question and a feature request.

In recent versions, Pandoc supports a new command line argument `--defaults=` with which a so-called ["defaults file"](https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#default-files) is specified. This file is in YAML format and makes it possible to configure all aspects of the Pandoc conversion process in a single file (apart from the template, which is referenced from the defaults file), i.e. all command line options have YAML equivalents. For example, I have a file `~/.pandoc/defaults/beamer_pdf.yaml` which specifies how I like my Beamer slides to be generated:

````yaml
reader: markdown+hard_line_breaks
writer: beamer
template: modified.latex
pdf-engine: latexmk
pdf-engine-opt: "-pdfxe"
dpi: 72
variables:
  theme: metropolis
  themeoptions:
    - sectionpage=simple
    - numbering=none
    - progressbar=foot
  mainfont: Fira Sans Regular
  mainfontoptions:
    - BoldFont={Fira Sans Medium}
  mathfont: Fira Math
  mathfontoptions:
    - math-style=ISO
    - bold-style=ISO
    - nabla=upright
    - partial=upright
    - Scale=1
  hyperrefoptions:
    - pdfpagemode=UseNone
````

I can now create Beamer slides from a Markdown file with the simple command

````
pandoc --defaults=beamer_pdf.yaml slides.md --output slides.pdf
````

I have several such defaults files for different kinds of outputs.

I recently started using R, and I would now like to use my existing defaults files for R Markdown. The idea would be to create a new output format which could be used like this in the YAML block of an R Markdown file:

````yaml
---
title: xyz
author: abc
output:
  pandoc::defaults:
    file: beamer_pdf.yaml
...
````

Following the instructions in *R Markdown: The Definitive Guide* under [Fully custom formats](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/format-custom.html), my attempt was this; within a package `pandoc`:

````R
defaults <- function(file) {
  rmarkdown::output_format(
    knitr = rmarkdown::knitr_options(),
    pandoc = rmarkdown::pandoc_options(
      args = paste("--defaults", file, sep = "=")
    ),
    clean_supporting = FALSE
  )
}
````

This doesn't work, because the argument `to` of `pandoc_options` needs to be specified. I guess I could replicate the way Pandoc finds defaults files, find it myself, read the YAML and set the argument based on the value of `writer`.

To simulate that, second attempt:

````R
defaults <- function(file) {
  rmarkdown::output_format(
    knitr = rmarkdown::knitr_options(),
    pandoc = rmarkdown::pandoc_options(
      to = "beamer",
      args = paste("--defaults", file, sep = "=")
    ),
    clean_supporting = FALSE
  )
}
````

The resulting Pandoc command is

````
/usr/bin/pandoc +RTS -K512m -RTS test.knit.md --to beamer --from markdown+autolink_bare_uris+tex_math_single_backslash --output test.tex --defaults=beamer_pdf.yaml
````

Several problems:

- A default value of `from` has been used, which conflicts with my setting in the defaults file. I don't mind `autolink_bare_uris` and `tex_math_single_backslash`, but I do prefer to have `hard_line_breaks`. Well, I guess I could extract that, too, and set it explicitly. 

- The output file is specified with extension `.tex` instead of `.pdf`. I tried the argument `to = "pdf"` – then I get a pdf file, but also a `--to latex` command line option.

- The `--defaults` command line argument is at the end, which makes Pandoc ignore it for the most part.

__As a question:__ What do I have to do in order to get the exact necessary Pandoc command to use my defaults file?

__As a feature request:__ In case that proves impossible, I propose that it is made possible.

I am aware that I could probably achieve the equivalent of my defaults files by inheriting from an existing output format and overriding the right options. However, that would mean to duplicate the effort I have already put in my defaults files, and every time I change something in my defaults files I would have to do the corresponding changes in the R code. I'd rather have a simple-to-use output format in R Markdown, the complete behavior of which is defined by the YAML defaults file.

I believe that this might also be useful for other users, because they wouldn't have to create an R package with a custom function, but they would simply write a defaults file.

description:

----

This issue concerns the [BiocStyle](https://github.com/Bioconductor/BiocStyle/) package and producing a PDF vignette from R Markdown.  This issue has initially been tracked in https://github.com/Bioconductor/BiocStyle/issues/93 I'm happy to incorporate necessary changes into **BiocStyle**, but wanted to report the unexpected behaviour here.

Consider the following minimal Rmd file (referred to as `test.Rmd` below) using the `BiocStyle::pdf_document` output format:

```r
---
title: "Vignette Title"
output:
  BiocStyle::pdf_document:
    keep_tex: true
---

Using the `images = "lowres"` is fine.
```

```r
rmarkdown::render("test.Rmd")
#> ...
#> Output created: test.pdf
```

However it fails when supply an `output_file` argument.  (In the example below I've used `test1.pdf` to distinguish between files, but it fails with the same error even if you use is the same as the default i.e. `test.pdf`).

```r
rmarkdown::render("test.Rmd", output_file = "test1.pdf")
#> ....
#> ! Package soul Error: Reconstruction failed.
```

Examining the two TeX files produced, the line containing the inline code differs, and seems to have some escaped spaces in the version that fails to compile.  The two lines are show below for comparison.  

```tex
Using the \texttt{images = "lowres"} is fine.   %Compiles
Using the \texttt{images\ =\ "lowres"} is fine. %Does not compile
```

Normally **BiocStyle** is aware of this issue and attempts to remove the escaped spaces before Latex is called.  However this patch is not applied when we specify the name of an output file with ".pdf" extension.

I believe the difference in output starts with the following code block:

https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/0af6b3556adf6e393b2da23c66c695724ea7bd2d/R/render.R#L487-L491

In our example where `output_file` is unspecified then it will be assigned `test.tex` (the value of `output_auto`) with the file extension reflecting the definition in `output_format$pandoc$ext`.  When we provide `output_file = "test1.pdf"` as an argument it obviously has ".pdf" as the extension.

This then affects the following code block, which is executed only in the case where we've specified `output_file = "test1.pdf"`:

https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/0af6b3556adf6e393b2da23c66c695724ea7bd2d/R/render.R#L974-L982

In the case of `output_file = "test1.pdf"` the latex compilation is carried out immediately at this step via `latexmk()` and fails due to something in the **BiocStyle** template.  However when `output_file` has a ".tex" extension compilation is deferred and carried out as part of `output_format$post_processor`, which also patches the template issues.  This is based on the technique used in **bookdown**.

---

Hopefully the above makes sense!  I'm not sure if we're doing something unsupported in **BiocStyle** but it seems the crux of this issue is that specifying the output file name will override the setting defined by our `output_format$pandoc`, and cause latex compilation to happen earlier than it otherwise would.  I wanted to check whether this is the expected behaviour.  I believe the issue is also present (but silently works) if you use `output_format = bookdown::pdf_document2`.  There `latexmk()` will be called twice - once in `render()` and once in the `output_format$post_processor.` with the second overwriting the first.

---

title: shinyApp / flexdashboard height issues
avoid hard requirement on shiny 1.6.0?
description:
The RStudio IDE relies on the `rmarkdown` package for a number of its integrated features, and generally we try to track the latest-available version of `rmarkdown`. However, this can cause issues for users who have projects relying on older versions of R packages. In particular, a large number of users might want to use the latest version of the RStudio IDE together with older projects using (for example) older versions of the `shiny` package.

It looks like a dependency on Shiny 1.6.0 was taken for `shiny::getCurrentTheme()` here:

https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/commit/9dc5d971f686d4a64ee7579117f78e648ec17a1f

Would it be possible to:

1. Roll back the hard version requirement on shiny 1.6.0, and
2. Make this piece of code conditional on shiny 1.6.0 being available / loaded?

This is of course assuming that the rest of the `rmarkdown` package can still function as expected with older versions of shiny; I'm not sure if any other changes have been made that rely on a newer version of shiny being available.

Arguably the onus is on RStudio to more properly fine-tune where and how we require specific versions of the `rmarkdown` package, but if this feels reasonably simple to change in the `rmarkdown` package itself then I believe it would make our lives easier.

Ref: https://github.com/rstudio/rstudio/pull/9847

title: strange behaviour with TeX conditionals
description:
I've upgraded my OS to Big Sur and am experiencing strange behaviour with RMarkdown documents that include TeX conditionals. This same computer previously had no issues with them (two documents I update regularly include similar conditionals). A reproducible example follows.

This Rmd code knits fine and produces a pdf that looks normal.
```
---
header-includes:
output: 
  pdf_document: 
    latex_engine: lualatex
---

This is a document to test whether RStudio can knit in TeX. It can.
```

In contrast, this Rmd code fails with the following error.
```
---
header-includes:
 - \newif\ifFlag
output: 
  pdf_document: 
    keep_tex: true
    latex_engine: lualatex
---

\Flagtrue

This is a document to test whether RStudio can knit in TeX with conditional statements.

\ifFlag
Flag is set to TRUE.
\else
Flag is set to FALSE.
\fi

The preceding test is enclosed in an ifelse statement.
```

Here is the error text:
```
! Emergency stop.
<*> tex_ifelse-test.tex

Error: LaTeX failed to compile tex_ifelse-test.tex. See https://yihui.org/tinytex/r/#debugging for debugging tips. See tex_ifelse-test.log for more info.
Execution halted
```

When I inspect the raw TeX created from the Rmd, it's clear why it's not rendering. Here is the relevant section of code:
```
\newif\ifFlag
\ifLuaTeX
  \usepackage{selnolig}  % disable illegal ligatures
\fi

\begin{document}

\def\iffalse\iftrue

This is a document to test whether RStudio can knit in TeX with
conditional statements.

\iftrue

Flag is set to TRUE. \else Flag is set to FALSE. \fi

The preceding test is enclosed in an ifelse statement.

\end{document}
```

As you can see, the if-else logic doesn't make any sense. This is new behavior after my macOS upgrade and it sort of baffles me ... why would this and only this be affected? (Several other Rmd documents I work with regularly knit fine, but only those with TeX conditionals fail).

This is in RStudio 2021.09.1 Build 372, freshly installed, with a fresh install of MacTeX. Any ideas?

title: `rmarkdown::render` fails when code chunks contain `sink(...)`
description:
## Context
I am writing a package that implements a standardized logging function using `sink(...)`. I would like to be able to use RMarkdown to write the vignettes for the package.

## Issue
Code chunks containing `sink(...)` commands do not sink if not followed in the same ~~line~~ *expression* by a `sink()` command closing the new connection. This is due to `evaluate`'s use of `sink()` to capture output. See issue opened with `evaluate`: https://github.com/r-lib/evaluate/issues/104

See also this relevant Stack Overflow issue: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/39131017/sink-wont-print-output-to-text-file-in-rmarkdown

## Proposed resolution
One option would be to modify the `evaluate` package so that these conditions throw an error and then have `rmarkdown` handle that error with either a warning to the user or by executing the `sink(...)` statement with `eval()`.

Alternately `rmarkdown` could identify offending statements separately.

## Reprex

Submit the following Rmd file via `rmarkdown::render()` or by clicking the "knit" button in Rstudio:
````
---
title: "Untitled"
output: html_document
---

# Log `sessionInfo()`

```{r}

title: Add support for svg in pdf_document
description:
Since 4 years ago, Pandoc is capable of including svg in pdf by internally using `rsvg_convert`.

https://github.com/jgm/pandoc/blame/fd7c140cde7544c0236586e2aa22691c33c3265a/src/Text/Pandoc/PDF.hs#L202

However, **rmarkdown** do not benefit it because we convert Rmd to TeX by pandoc, and then TeX to PDF by latexmk since  #1222 (v1.9). Note that we can include svg if we use rmarkdown 1.8. See example below.

I feel the support is very useful when we output multiple formats supporting svg (e.g., html and pdf).
I suggest adding the feature by calling `rsvg_convert` from a lua filter.

````
---
output: pdf_document
---

```{r}
ggplot2::ggsave(
  "example.svg",
  ggplot2::qplot(1, 1)
)
```
````

title: [FR] Interrupted lists are merged into a continuous list
description:
<!--
- Provide a clear and concise description of the problem this proposed feature would address? 
- Try to detail what you want to happen.
- Have you thought of alternative solutions or workarounds you've considered ? We'll be glad to know about them!
- Any other context or screenshots about your feature request that would help us understand ? Please include them!
-->

# Problem
A list whose numbering continues after interruption is created as:
```
   (@) element 1
   (@) element 2
------interruption----
   (@) element 3
   (@) element 4
```

The problem is when including more than one such list in document, they are treated as a single interrupted list: their numbering is merged. Example:
```
List 1:

   (@) element 1
   (@) element 2
------interruption----
   (@) element 3
   (@) element 4

Some very long paragraphs and code chunks.
List 2:

   (@) element 5
   (@) element 6
```

Interruption is undefined, so the numbering of an list is continuous with that of the previous list. 

# Suggestions
1. As with tabsets, using `(@) {-}` after each interrupted list to may mark it's end, so the numbering of any further list of the same type is independent of it's previous cousin. This approach is simpler than the next.
2. Maybe we can use an ID for each list, where the list ID is placed in the `(@)` itself. Example: 
```
List 1:

   (@1) element 1
   (@1) element 2
------interruption----
   (@1) element 3
   (@1) element 4

Some very long paragraphs and code chunks.
List 2:

   (@2) element 1
   (@2) element 2
```
This may be helpful for overlapping lists, where we might want the numbering of a list to be continuous with a specific list, which might not be the previous one. Example:
```
List 1:

   (@1) element 1
   (@1) element 2

--interruption----
List 2:

   (@2) element 1
   (@2) element 1

---- interruption----

List 1 continuous: 

   (@1) element 3
   (@1) element 4
```

An ID may be anything not only a numeric. 
This approach isn't as simple as the first but may be of use in very limited cases. However, these limited cases may be ubiquitous in some industries or some fields in academia, so you might consider it.


Warmly

title: [FR] Add an implicit inline function to overwrite formatting of selected text
description:
<!--
- Provide a clear and concise description of the problem this proposed feature would address?
- Try to detail what you want to happen.
- Have you thought of alternative solutions or workarounds you've considered ? We'll be glad to know about them!
- Any other context or screenshots about your feature request that would help us understand ? Please include them!
-->

Related to #2233 issue on a suggested syntax to bulk-subscript a sentence.

# Overwrite formatting via `[text](<- )` shortcut
The main reason I use subscripts is to include a note that don't interfere with the main flow of ideas in a paragraph. Example: 
`The plot indicates a strong relationship between x & z, ~VS~ ~the~ ~minor~ ~relationship~ ~between~ ~x~ ~&~ ~y,~ which suggests bla bla bla`.  

An alternative to using subscripts, which I really have no idea whether it's around or not, is to use a smaller font for this note. A simple syntax I suggest is `[text](numeric)`, where the numeric is the absolute text size, or if has an explicit sign like in the example, the relative text size. It look like this:
`The plot indicates a strong relationship between x & z, [VS the minor relationship between x & y](-2) which suggests bla bla bla`.

Here `-2` isn't a hyperlink or so, being totally **numeric** helps differentiate it from a link, which as far as I know must include characters. This -2 might by interpreted as the difference between the font size of the paragraph & the font size of text [enclosed in such brackets], or the relative size of the text output. 
This particular syntax might require editing a lot of existing code, so another syntax may be preferred. I just find this one convenient & will allow effortless control over the text output. 

If this syntax is implemented, a relevant feature might by changing the color of a text  or its background verbatim color. For example using:
`[some text](<- col = "blue")`
Where the `<-` operator may be interpreted as  an indicator that differentiates the characters in these parentheses from a link. A function may be defined to overwrite formatting of output text, which may be called implicitly whenever a text is enclosed in brackets with the `<-` operator placed in the very start of the parentheses. Formatting arguments not passed into the `(<- )` call are not changed.

# No confusion
So, an aggregation to the bulk-subscript suggestion, we might have:
- `[text](characters)` indicating a link.
- `[text](#characters)` indicating a link within the document.
- `[text](<- some formatting arguments)` to over-write the formatting of the text output.
- `[text](numeric)` as a shortcut of the format overwriting function to just change the size of enclosed text.

Finally, you guys are amazing and rmarkdown is really making my life tremendously easier. I can't thank you enough. 

Warmly

title: [FR] New syntax to bulk-subscript a selection of words
description:
<!--

- Provide a clear and concise description of the problem this proposed feature would address? 
- Try to detail what you want to happen.
- Have you thought of alternative solutions or workarounds you've considered ? We'll be glad to know about them!
- Any other context or screenshots about your feature request that would help us understand ? Please include them!

-->

# The problem: subscript tedious syntax
I wrote my first rmarkdown report recently and was very annoyed as I had a lot of sentences as subscripts. I wrote them like:
`~this is a subscript~`. However, the rendered output was exactly as the input. I reconsulted the cheat sheet, [R Markdown: The Definitive Guide](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/) and [R Markdown Cookbook](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/). I didn't see the problem. 

Finally, using minimal trial and error, I understood that each word must be wrapped in 2 tildes. The right input is: `~this~ ~is~ ~a~ ~subscript~`.  Re writing all the subscripted sentences for a 1000 lines documents was painful.

# Suggestions
1. To include a two-word example in the cheat sheet instead of `~2~`. For example: `~Hello,~ ~world!~`. This indicates that the number of tildes must be twice the number of spaces between words. 
2. A better syntax may be: `[~this is a subscript~]` , which may be automatically replaced with `~this~ ~is~ ~a~ ~subscript~` and rendered as a subscript. I believe this conversion before rendering will cause no inconvenient events with community formats or so. 

This syntax can serve different purposes, each of which has an associated symbol. Meaning, `[~some text~]` outputs a subscript, `[^some text^]` may output a superscript, and so on.

Another more broad-scope suggestion is in this related issue: #2234

Warmly

title: [FR] Support simple dynamic runtime without shiny
description:
Current `rmarkdown::render` function supports 4 runtime options

```
$runtime
c("auto", "static", "shiny", "shinyrmd", "shiny_prerendered")
```

When I was trying to embed some htmlwidgets with no `self_contained` (large datasets: ~200MB 3D mesh files) under `static` runtime, the browser gives me CORS error. 

So I tried to run the document with `shinyrmd` and `shiny_prerendered`, the browser gave me JavaScript errors (basically JS object `Shiny` was not working as expected). The reason why this happened was because **`htmlwidgets` allowed the widgets to have different behaviors with/without shiny**. When the widgets detected shiny, they tried to call shiny input update functions, but since `shiny` behaved different than the normal dashboard mode, JS error was raised.

Would it be possible to have dynamic runtime, but without shiny?


[PS]: I also tried `shiny` runtime out of curiosity, but got C Stack error.

title: segfaults inside shiny inside shinytest when rmarkdown is involved
description:
(Cross-post from https://github.com/thomasp85/patchwork/issues/278 after finding that rmarkdown 2.10 seems to work.)

I have a problem that is very delicate to reproduce. The only way I can reproduce it, though with varying success, is by plotting a some `patchwork` inside an Rmd file which is rendered using `rmarkdown::render()` in the download handler of a `shiny` app tested using `shinytest`. However, running the Shiny app itself works fine, and so far, I have not found a way to remove anything meaningful from the Shiny app, or the problem stops to show. Due to the stochastic nature of the problem, it is challenging to draw hard conclusions. One thing that I noticed by taking apart `shinytest::testApp`, however, that the problem became more severe by this construct:

```r
    env <- new.env(parent = .GlobalEnv)
    source(testname, local = env)
```
https://github.com/rstudio/shinytest/blob/d0f6d737919b542c6a1e8bbd0ea05f9e4b3f5334/R/test-app.R#L65-L66

The problem started after I changed a bunch of code before the `patchwork` calls - but the output of this changed piece of code is not used in the `patchwork` at all, and is identical to the output before the change. I can go back in time using version control to a point where the problem never shows, and then gradually change my code again to make the problem appear more and more often.

I collected some 10 stack traces, all of which hint at `patchwork` or `grid`. But it is not impossible that other packages are involved.

I then tried `devtools::install_version("rmarkdown", "2.10")`, and all of a sudden, the problem is gone. The differences between 2.10 and 2.11 are small, see https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/compare/v2.10...v2.11, but one thing caught my eye - this:

https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/b218cd79c2e102e8149fb029718d37129dae865c/R/shiny_prerendered.R#L123-L126

introduced in https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/commit/b218cd79c2e102e8149fb029718d37129dae865c

This may be a total coincidence, but it may also not - that's why I am crossposting here. I also don't know if that commit is an actual bug or just unearths another one, but maybe someone here knows how to proceed in such a case.

title: [FR] `self_contained: false` html dependency cache
description:
Hi all,

Is there any way to allow for caching of Rmarkdown JS dependencies in a lib_dir? I can put together a reprex, but it seems like each time you render a document using `self_contained: false` it overwrites dependencies, without checking whether they already exist. I can understand why this wouldn't always be ideal, but other times (during editing or when rendering 10 or more Rmd's iteratively) it can be quite time-consuming. 

I'm happy to help on the dev side, was curious to get some initial thoughts.

title: runtime: shinyrmd always renders at startup
description:
The 2.11 rmarkdown release (as well as the latest code) always re-renders the HTML before starting the Shiny HTTP server. This is a regression from 2.10 and earlier, which would re-render the HTML only if it was seen as out-dated (per `rmarkdown:::shiny_prerendered_prerender`).

Given the following `server.Rmd` and `server.R`:

````markdown
---
title: "server.Rmd: rendered at most once"
runtime: shinyrmd
---

This document can be slow for the first client. The R code block is evaluated
at render-time, which occurs at most once, and only when the HTML does not
already exist. When the HTML already exists, there is no render cost.

```{r}
Sys.sleep(1)
```
````

```r
# server.R that pairs with server.Rmd.
function(input, output) {}
```

Run this document, stop the server, then check if we see a pre-render as still necessary.

```r
# This call to run() will render "server.html" and then start a Shiny server.
# Stop the Shiny server once it starts listening.
rmarkdown::run(file = "./server.Rmd")

# Check to see if a pre-render is still needed:
rmarkdown:::shiny_prerendered_prerender("./server.Rmd", "./server.html", ".", "1")
# => TRUE

# Perform another call to run(); this will run another render of "server.html"
# before starting the Shiny server.
rmarkdown::run(file = "./server.Rmd")
```

In rmarkdown-2.10, the call to `rmarkdown:::shiny_prerendered_prerender` returns `FALSE` and the second call to `rmarkdown::run` does not perform a render. This is correct; `rmarkdown::run` should not render when its inputs are unchanged.

In rmarkdown-2.11, the call to `rmarkdown:::shiny_prerendered_prerender` returns `TRUE` and the second call to `rmarkdown::run` performs an unnecessary render of the HTML. This is a difference from the previous release; the document is unchanged.

It appears as if the following block of code is returning `TRUE` because we are detecting inconsistent package dependencies (when I run, `depPkg="jquerylib"` is seen as having a `depVer=NULL`, which is enough to trigger the render.
https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/61a4cc7a5a3ed821f7fe208874adcb980da8de94/R/shiny_prerendered.R#L256-L290


```

title: [FR] - Update the `variant` parameter documentation for `md_document`
description:
## The Problem

It looks like the [documentation for an `md_document`'s markdown variant][1] has fallen out of step with the [actual implementation][2]. If we compare the documented parameters to the ones in the current source code as of this writing, it looks like the undocumented options are `commonmark` and `commonmark_x`:

| [In the book][1]  | [In the source code][2] |
| ----------------- | ----------------------- |
| markdown          | gfm                     |
| markdown_strict   | commonmark              |
| markdown_github   | commonmark_x            |
| markdown_mmd      | markdown                |
| markdown_phpextra | markdown_phpextra       |
|                   | markdown_github         |
|                   | markdown_strict         |

This discrepancy leads me to a few questions.

1. Is `commonmark_x` meant to be something user-facing?
2. Should there be an `rmarkdown` variant?

I know question 2 might seem silly: your source file *is* Rmarkdown, so why would you want to specify the output as Rmarkdown? But, it would be nice to have one variant that represents all the markdown extensions that Rmarkdown uses, so I wouldn't have to manually specify them if I want to make a clean plaintext export.

## Example Use Case

I'm writing a manuscript in Rmarkdown. I'm currently using the RMarkdown Visual Editor with [sentence-level line wrapping](https://rstudio.github.io/visual-markdown-editing/markdown.html?q=canonical#line-wrapping). The result is a manuscript where single paragraphs are broken across multiple lines. This line wrapping is great for fine-grained version control to track changes, but it doesn't look nice to read.

What I'd love is an easy way to specify turning this document into an Rmarkdown document that wraps at the paragraph-level.

Thanks!

[1]: https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/markdown-document.html#markdown-variants
[2]: https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/0af6b3556adf6e393b2da23c66c695724ea7bd2d/R/md_document.R#L111-L129

title: [FR] Offer a new syntax to create verbatim code chunks from Pandoc
description:
## What's new ? 

Writing verbatim code chunk in Rmarkdown document would be possible like this

`````markdown
````{.markdown}
```{{r setup, echo=TRUE}}
library(tidyverse)
```
````
`````
or 

`````markdown
````markdown
```{{r setup, echo=TRUE}}
library(tidyverse)
```
````
`````

Basically, syntax would be using `{{ }}` instead of simple `{ }` instead of current `` `r ''` `` trick 
(https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/verbatim-code-chunks.html) 

## How ?  

This would be made possible using a Lua filter

* knitr won't parse this part of the Rmd source
* Pandoc will create a Codeblock element with the content
* The Lua filter will replace the text content inside this CodeBlock ```{{r setup, echo=TRUE}} by ```{r setup, echo=TRUE} using a regex + gsub. This will create a code block of the language class set in the external backticks to show as-is a knitr code chunk with engine an option.


See discussion for details : https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/1688#issuecomment-908565459

cc @apreshill

title: Allow use of shiny widgets with the "shiny_prerendered" runtime [FR]
description:
Currently, Rmd notebooks using `shiny_prerendered` cannot utilize shiny widgets as far as I can tell. For example:


```
    ---
    title: "example"
    output: html_document
    runtime: shiny_prerendered
    ---


    ```{r setup}
    library(rmdexamples)
    ```
    
    ```{r, context = "render"}
    kmeans_cluster(iris)
    ```
```

While this will render a static image of the UI, it will not be interactive. Changing the context to `server` or `server-start` results in no loading of the UI. Changing it to `data` results in a static image as well.

A way to utilize data caching alongside Shiny widgets in Rmd files would be very useful.

title: lib_dir without dependency versioning: allowing HTML files generated at different points in time with different rmarkdown versions to use same lib_dir
description:
Currently, a Rmarkdown file rendered to HTML with option `lib_dir: libs` will create a libs folder with the dependencies, appended by their version names e.g. 'bootstrap-3.3.5', 'jquery-1.11.3', which are linked in the header of the generated HTML file. This means, that if I generate another Rmarkdown file at a different point in time, and I want it to use the same `lib_dir`, say, because I want to place these HTML documents jointly inside a directory on a server with a libs subdirectory containing the libraries, then only a minor version change of any of these libraries inhibit my new HTML file to display properly on my server, simply because the version number in the folder name changed. 

I would thus like to request an option to omit version numbers from the folder names in dependencies together with option `lib_dir` e.g. so that the folders are named `bootstrap` and `jquery` and not 'bootstrap-3.3.5' and 'jquery-1.11.3'.

It is clear that open source software is evolving and that this will at some point cause code to break, or, in this case, HTML outputs to display in a wrong way. However, most of the time minor version changes of major libraries do not break much at all. With the current naming of dependency folders, a minor version change breaks code by design, and the only way around it is a totally unnecessary duplication of the dependencies for each new Rmarkdown file generated for serving from the web. 

So having an option allowing generic dependency names and linking would be much more conducive to people wanting to serve multiple Rmarkdown files off a web-server.

title: Provide a syntax definition file with updated support for R new syntax
description:
First issue has been reported in rstudio/bookdown#1157.  See discussion there for details. In a nutshell: 
* Pandoc's highlighting uses KDE XML syntax file 
* the KDE XML syntax file for R language does not correctly handles the new R syntax. 

Current fix in **rmarkdown** is for `html_document_base()` only as a post processing - see https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/commit/99df4e7db5ba0108c51557639e661df05554bf1b . This fixes the issue rstudio/bookdown#1157

Proper fix should be: 

* Push upstream correct support for Pandoc for later Pandoc's version.
* Use the XML definition file directly in **rmarkdown** for previous pandoc version that won't have the updated support, using `--syntax-definition` flag.
