title: Incremental graphs
description:
When I'm making a presentation, I often want to build up my graphs incrementally, so that the viewer can parse them a little at a time. It's especially useful when giving a "surprise" result to first show the graph without the surprise, then add the surprise.

It is, of course, possible to do this in ioslides by simply copying and pasting multiple similar slides. But that's poor style; it violates DRY, and so for every small format change you want to make on the graph, you have to copy and "re-merge" the change for each of the copied slides.

I've added two functions, gginc and stages, to make this easier to do cleanly. I've also tweaked the javascript and css for ioslides to support this. The same basic idea could be applied to the other presentation output formats, but I've just done ioslides for now.

I don't think it's really a good idea to have this change exist as a separate package, given that it must integrate at the level of javascript and css.

title: Proposed feature: rmarkdown::custom_knit`
description:
There's currently an undocumented ability to specify a `knit:` hook in Rmarkdown YAML headers and replace `rmarkdown::render` with something else in RStudio, as used for example in [slidify](https://github.com/ramnathv/slidify/commit/07794a3c2d228822c173c1ad5eacf5ab54a42062#diff-1), and which I describe further potential uses for in notes [here](https://github.com/lmmx/devnotes/wiki/Rmarkdown-custom-knit-hook-to-compile-a-multi-part-document).

This could provide a sort of `make` for Rmarkdown, with metadata-directed knitting of e.g. files that may be added through `includes:` in YAML headers, or as `{r child=...}` code chunk references within the document itself (see notes linked above for examples, and [this repository](https://github.com/lmmx/tomasetti-vogelstein-2015)).

Although a Knit button running the above is user-friendly, it's natural to want to be able to replicate the button's behaviour as a command, which I presume would be best placed in the `rmarkdown` package (thus available within RStudio by default).

@cboettig recommended in [this thread](https://github.com/ropensci/reproducibility-guide/pull/81#issuecomment-76936284) that there should be a way to call said custom function from the command-line.

I recommend a function e.g. `rmarkdown::custom_knit` :

``` r
custom_knit <- function(filename, encoding) {
    rmd.content <-  paste( readLines(filename) , sep = "\n" )
    yaml.range <- which('---' == rmd.content)[1:2]
    if (all(is.na(yaml.range))) { knit.function <- rmarkdown::render } else {
        yaml.header.range <- setdiff(do.call(seq, as.list(yaml.range)), yaml.range)
        rmd.yaml <- paste(rmd.content[yaml.header.range], collapse="\n")
        knit.hook <- yaml::yaml.load(rmd.yaml)$knit
        if (is.null(knit.hook)) {knit.function <- rmarkdown::render} else { 
            knit.func.str <- as.function(as.list(knit.hook))()
            knit.function <- eval(parse(text = call(knit.func.str)))
        }
    }
    return(knit.function(filename, encoding = encoding))
}
```

Running the function on for example the 'analysis.Rmd' file of [this example repo](https://github.com/lmmx/tomasetti-vogelstein-2015):

``` r
custom_knit('documents/analysis.Rmd', 'UTF-8')
```

would then run the same as the button in RStudio.
- The above handles both anonymous functions and those sourced as `package::function` (e.g. test with `knit: slidify::knit2slides` in YAML of `analysis.Rmd`). If no `knit:` hook is present it uses `rmarkdown::render` as the knit function.
- Do others feel it would be better suited to a modification of another function, e.g. as behaviour triggered by a parameter in some existing function? e.g.
  
  ``` r
  render(input, encoding, custom_knit = TRUE)
  ```

title: support long-form output
description:
Rmarkdown is fantastic, but (other than PDF via LaTeX), it seems a little lacking in publishing long-form stuff like a book.
I am aware of @yihui's great [Rmarkdown vs LaTeX](http://yihui.name/en/2013/10/markdown-or-latex/) piece, and I agree that if floats and _typesetting_ on a physical piece of paper are key, it's probably easier to start with LaTeX and `.rnw` to begin with.

If you're _not_ into paper, however, there's nothing Rmarkdown can't do for you (ok, maybe except for indexed tables, figures etc. #382 :).

The only thing missing for fully digital publishing from this fantastic [Rmarkdown](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/) / [Pandoc](https://github.com/jgm/pandoc) / [Knitr](https://github.com/yihui/knitr) toolchain is an easy way to deploy long-form pieces to the web.

Several alternative / additional ways of how to do this come to mind.
- Go via [Jekyll](https://github.com/jekyll/jekyll)
  Have an `output_options =  "Jekyll"`, where `render` wraps a bunch of `*.md`s in a directory ready to be published via Jekyll.
  Maybe have 1-2 suitable Jekyll templates that would make the result look suitably book-like (chapter and section navigation, etc.).
  The nice thing would be that many people already have their work on github, and if `render` could somehow write the result to the `gh-pages` branch you'd have your book up and running in two commands. (`render`, `push`)
- Go via [gitbook.io](https://github.com/GitbookIO/gitbook)
  These guys have made a really pretty UI.
  An `output_options = "Gitbook.io"` would simply place all of the `*.md`s appropriately in a directory and create an additional `SUMMARY.MD` as specified by gitbook.io.
  Getting this stuff online would be a tad more difficult though, but I guess it could also be done in `gitbook-io` branch of some project.
  I have raised an issue with gitbook.io about *.Rmd support -> https://github.com/GitbookIO/gitbook/issues/307
- There is also [softcover](https://github.com/softcover/softcover)

I'm just curious what other people think about this / how they go about this.

title: get more editor support
description:
I love `rmarkdown`, and I think as a format, it may just finally solve a lot of problems in academic / data-driven publishing (LaTeX being great, but paper-focused and unwieldy).

There's just one thing that's holding me back a little: Rmarkdown seems a little ... RStudio-y, meaning, if you don't use RStudio,  a lot of support (syntax highlighting, REPL, build functions etc.) are gone.

I understand that this is an open source project and that I (nor anyone) isn't entitled to support of their favorite editor (or anything, really), but I still wanted to raise this issue and see what other people thought about it.

I've also raised a [package suggestion for atom.io](https://discuss.atom.io/t/package-suggestion-rmarkdown/15074), but had little resonance so far.

There's also _some_ support in Sublime Text 3, via [R-Box](https://github.com/randy3k/R-Box) and (hopefully?) [AcademciMarkdown](https://github.com/mangecoeur/AcademicMarkdown), but it seems like both could use more help.

title: Error line numbers are wrong
description:
Sorry if this rather belongs in Rstudio.
Debugging Rmds was easier with knitr, because it sent you to the right line number when an error occurred. Now the default view is the "Issues" view in Rstudio. Not only is this view a bit cramped, it contains superfluous information (like the trace "Calls: <Anonymous> ... withCallingHandlers -> withVisible -> eval -> eval -> plot" – everything from Anonymous to plot is just related to knitr internals, I don't care about it and it confuses our B.Sc.s).
You cannot copy the entries in the Issues view.

The output view is more useful, but it only says `Quitting from lines 19-21 (test.Rmd)`, ie. it gives you only an approximate line number.
The line number in "Issues" is precise, but it can be completely off. One instance where I could pinpoint it: if I source an R script inside a chunk, all errors after the source statements will be pinned to the top of the chunk.

Here's a reproducible script:

``````
```{r}
source("~/Any_old_file.R")
plot(car)
```
``````

I hope bugs relating to this can be fixed and that debugging Rmds becomes easier in general.
I've had some fairly difficult to debug problems recently where these changes made them very tough to crack. 
Usually I simply execute a file with Command-Shift-S in a fresh session so that I can debug in the session.
This is not my favourite way though, because this way I don't benefit from the cache, and some of my Rmd files take hours to execute.

I would love to be able to pick up inside the session when rmarkdown errors out, I don't know if that's possible though.

title: Ability to set cairo_pdf as a default graphic device for pdf output
description:
pdf_cairo() has one big advantage over pdf() for non-english users - it supports national characters on Windows out of the box.

Obviously I can change default graphic device in the first chunk of my markdown document:

``` r
if(identical(opts_knit$get('rmarkdown.pandoc.to'), 'latex')){
  if(identical(capabilities()['cairo'], c('cairo' = TRUE))){
    opts_chunk$set('dev' = 'cairo_pdf')
  }
}
```

but an important reason you use rmarkdown is you do not have to take care of such things.

So maybe it will be worth to include an option to switch to pdf_cairo(), e.g. as an 

```
output: 
  pdf_document: 
    dev: [pdf/cairo_pdf]
```

option of the YAML section of a markdown document (and move the code above to the `rmarkdown::render()`).

By the way - it would be nice to be able to choose between PNG and SVG graphics in the HTML output in the same way.

title: sh: 1: /home/travis/opt/pandoc/pandoc: not found
description:
Rmarkdown is trying to find pandoc instead of just using `$PATH`.

the [`find_pandoc`](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/d4947c70cbbc7a588a18a71dfcbcabef0dba1412/R/pandoc.R#L487) function is supposed to find the Pandoc _executable_, which it does, using `Sys.which`.

Once found, `find_pandoc` tries to find pandoc's version [here](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/d4947c70cbbc7a588a18a71dfcbcabef0dba1412/R/pandoc.R#L501) using the function [`get_pandoc_version`](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/d4947c70cbbc7a588a18a71dfcbcabef0dba1412/R/pandoc.R#L527) which takes the location of the pandoc **binary** as first argument, but treats it as if it is the pandoc installation directory. It joins `pandoc` to the path of the binary (resulting in `pandoc/pandoc`) then tries to execute it crashing the program because the file does not exist.

I have a [`.travis.yml`](https://github.com/audy/make-rmarkdown/blob/5cb1d097b6c300fd436e3adc41ed256e62ee6f3c/.travis.yml) that reproduces this error.

Is there a way to override this or just use `$PATH`?

title: Documentation for upgrading site's Bootstrap library & dependent code
description:
Hi @jjallaire, thanks again for the upgrade the Bootstrap library used in `rmarkdown` and updating the CSS tags in the navigation bar (https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/issues/263).  I've copied most of your Jekyll/RMarkdown/CSS structure in a site of ours (http://ouhscbbmc.github.io/MReportingPublic/).

I don't know how many other people have ~~stolen~~ been inspired by that site like me.  But for those who have might, they be surprised the next time they upgrade the `rmarkdown` package.  I wrote these steps for a friend (whose also using the same structure for his site) to help him transition to the new Bootstrap version.  

If you're considering writing some transition notice, feel free to take any portion of this list that might help those users.
1. upgrade to the newest GitHub version of RMarkdown with devtools.  This is the main thing that makes it build with newest supported bootstrap version (currently 3.3.1 instead of 2.3.2).
2. The CSS in `include/before_body.html` has changed a lot.  It probably makes the most sense to copy the newest version from the RMarkdown site, then add your heading/links to it.  Trying to upgrade your existing menu structure's CSS would be pretty error-prone.
3. JJ also updated `include/in_header.html`.  I copied that too.
4. Delete the old bootstrap library code in `libs/`
5. The 'GitHub' button doesn't render properly on the menu any more.  The top alignment was 0 px, and I didn't see how to space it correctly.  So I put a button at the bottom of the index page instead.  I also put it in a well panel with a Zenodo DOI badge.
6. If you did any other custom stuff, it may need to change with the new version of Bootstrap. See http://bootswatch.com/ examples for the code.
7. Rebuild/rerender all the md files into html, with your typical process.  Then push to the GitHub server.

For an example, see the three Dec 21 commits in https://github.com/LiveOak/NlsyLinks/commits/gh-pages.

title: Documenting functions
description:
To a large degree, I try to do my analyses by writing functions that do the heavy lifting. Furthermore, following Carl Boettiger's lead, I am starting to write these functions as packages (enforces at least minimal documentation, more easily shareable and reusable).

The challenge is how to document the functions, for example in a way that would be useful to include in the appendix to a paper. When I am creating a package as part of an analysis project, I use Rogyen comments to provide input to Rd files; but this represents functional documentation, rather than line-by-line explanation of the underlying code. The best I have found for the latter is to write simple R comments within the code.

It would be really nice to be able to generate a document that is the formatted Rd documentation for a function followed by the function's code itself, based on an R file that had the Rd documentation in Roxygen format along with the code.

It would be even nicer to be able to be able to also have formatted documentation _within_ the function's code listing. As far as I can tell, Roxygen-style comments are not converted to markdown by render() when they are inside a function. 

Similarly, when I am defining a function in a standalone Rmd document, it would be nice to be able to intersperse explanatory text within the function body - but as far as I have been able to tell, the entire function definition has to be within a single code chunk.

I realize that breaking up a function definition with formatted documentation renders the intervening code chunks incomplete, which perhaps violates one of your core design philosophies. But I think it could be useful for publication support documents. 

More selfishly, my immediate motivation is communicating with collaborators who are not fluent in R (simultaneously explaining my code and showing off the self-documenting potential of R that might override counteract anti-R biases that come primarily from modest differences in execution speed).

I realize that the solution to these requests may not be incremental. I can imagine that the simpler version (Rd documentation + code listing) might be achieved with a flag to render() that indicates that the comment blocks should be passed through roxygenize() for conversion to suitably formatted documentation, but I don't know enough about the underlying processes to know whether that is simple or hard. If all this is way out of scope feel free to ask me to go away...

Thanks for all you do! Rmarkdown is finally getting me to write well-documented code...

title: feature request: Rscript-like front end for render()
description:
It feels like `rmarkdown::render()` is missing an idiom for passing command line arguments.

Consider a recipe you might put into a `Makefile` to run an R script in a pipeline:

`Rscript foo.R january.csv`

where you might have lines like `options <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE); data_file <- options[1]` inside `foo.R`, so you can apply whatever brilliant processing `foo.R` does to data from different months.

Now imagine, you prefer to run R scripts and RMarkdown files with `rmarkdown::render()` instead because you like the side effect of getting Markdown and/or HTML reports along with the primary outputs.

Now your `make` recipes start to look more like this:

``` Makefile
Rscript -e 'library(rmarkdown); data_file <- "$(DATA_FILE)"; render("$<", quiet = TRUE)'
```

assuming you're using `Make`'s command line arguments to set the variable `DATA_FILE`. (_The recipe inevitably goes on to do a lot of file renaming and moving because `render()` is pretty wonky about specifying destination and intermediate directories other than source directory -- e.g. #286, #285, #236, #130_).

I'm not sure what solution I'm even asking for re: command line argument emulation for `rmarkdown::render()`. But `render()` is becoming my preferred way to run things and I'm interested in making that less awkward. Would appreciate any thoughts.

@sjackman do you have anything to add?

title: Understanding `_output.yaml` in generating websites
description:
Pandoc has the very convenient feature of being able to specify an external yaml file to provide metadata that would be re-used across multiple files; as shown in the docs:

```
pandoc chap1.md chap2.md chap3.md metadata.yaml -s -o book.html
```

At first I'd imagined that this is how `_output.yaml` was working too, but at closer inspection it appears that's not the case.  This is rather frustrating as it was very convenient to be able to define arbitrary template metadata in a `metadata.yaml` that I could then use in custom templates (e.g. rather analogous to _config.yaml in Jekyll).  Unfortunately, if I just create an `_output.yaml` like this:

``` yaml
html_document:
  self_contained: false
  css: 
    - http://www.carlboettiger.info/assets/css/bootstrap.min.css
    - //netdna.bootstrapcdn.com/font-awesome/4.0.3/css/font-awesome.css
rss: http://www.carlboettiger.info/blog.xml
rss-title: "Carl Boettiger's Lab Notebook"
site.url: http://carlboettiger.info
analytics: UA-XXXXXX-1 
author: 
  name: Carl Boettiger
  twitter: cboettig
  github: cboettig
```

it seems some variables, like css, are recognized, but arbitrary template variables like `author.twitter` are not (whether or not they are nested under `html_document`).  If instead I run pandoc directly and use the above `yaml` file as an external metadata block like in the `metadata.yaml` case illustrated above, everything works.  Would it be possible for rmarkdown to support something like this?

title: bash code with non-zero exit status in last statement causes backtrace.
description:
Here are three tests of using engine='bash' coe blocks.  The third one shows the bug:
- first one works quite nicely:

``` r test1, engine='bash'
echo one
echo two
echo three
```

rendering as:

```
## one
## two
## three
```
- second one hows that  non-zero returns generally get a fair treatment:

``` r test2, engine='bash'
ECHO one
ECHO two
echo three
```

rendering reasonably (though the reporting seems a little uneven), like this:

```
## bash: ECHO: command not found
## bash: line 1: ECHO: command not found
## three
```
- alas, third one reveals a PROBLEM when the LAST statement returns non-zero status, as in:

``` r test3, engine='bash'
echo one
echo two
ECHO three
```

because output is not generated and we get a R backtrace, like this:

```
running: bash  -c 'echo one
echo two
ECHO three'
Quitting from lines 3-6 (foo.Rmd)

[[2]]
render("/home/mec/project/ODR/doc/foo.Rmd", "all")

[[3]]
knitr::knit(knit_input, knit_output, envir = envir, quiet = quiet,
    encoding = encoding)

[[4]]
process_file(text, output)

[[5]]
withCallingHandlers(if (tangle) process_tangle(group) else process_group(group),
    error = function(e) {
        setwd(wd)
        cat(res, sep = "\n", file = output %n% "")
        message("Quitting from lines ", paste(current_lines(i),
            collapse = "-"), " (", knit_concord$get("infile"),
            ") ")
    })

[[6]]
process_group(group)

[[7]]
process_group.block(group)

[[8]]
call_block(x)

[[9]]
block_exec(params)

[[10]]
in_dir(opts_knit$get("root.dir") %n% input_dir(), (knit_engines$get(options$engine))(options))

[[11]]
(knit_engines$get(options$engine))(options)

[[12]]
system2(cmd, code, stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE)

[[13]]
.handleSimpleError(function (e)
print(sys.calls()), "error in running command", quote(system2(cmd,
    code, stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE)))

[[14]]
h(simpleError(msg, call))

Error in system2(cmd, code, stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE) :
  error in running command
Calls: withCallingHandlers ... call_block -> block_exec -> in_dir -> <Anonymous> -> system2

Execution halted

```

I expect the implementation has some confusion about handling the bash error.  I think the following example shows that even if there is a syntax error in the code that bash is passed, if bash successfully TRIES to execute the code and reports the error that the return value of the bash call should be 0:

``` sh
$bash -c 'echo  ee; echo $?'; echo $?
ee
0
0
$ bash -c 'ECHO  ee; echo $?'; echo $?
bash: ECHO: command not found
127
0
```

I further expect that the implementation might benefit from passing the code block to `bash` on stdin instead of using -c.

title: Missing value for `pandoc_variable_arg`
description:
Pandoc command-line variables can optionally define values for a variable, but the value is required for `pandoc_variable_arg`.

``` r
pandoc_variable_arg("varname") # should produce c("--variable","varname")
# Error in paste(name, "=", value, sep = "") : 
#  argument "value" is missing, with no default
```

title: Path arguments do not have the expected values.
description:
Path arguments are lazily evaluated _after_ the working directory is changed, so any use of e.g. `normalizePath` resolves relative to the _new_ working directory, not the _old_ working directory.

Example:

``` r
# This creates an output at path/to/source/path/to/even/deeper/output/tst.html
render("path/to/source/tst.Rmd",
  intermediates_dir = {normalizePath("path/intermediate/")},
  output_dir = {normalizePath("path/to/even/deeper/output/")},
  clean=TRUE)

# Whereas this creates it at path/to/even/deeper/output/tst.html
intermediates_dir = {normalizePath("path/intermediate/")};
output_dir = {normalizePath("path/to/even/deeper/output/")}
render("path/to/source/tst.Rmd",
  intermediates_dir = intermediates_dir,
  output_dir = output_dir,clean=TRUE)
```

title: The `render` paths are relative to the input directory
description:
The `intermediates_dir` and `output_dir` directories are relative to the input path, not the working directory.

You can make that work with this:

``` r
render("path/to/source/tst.Rmd",
  intermediates_dir = "../../../path/intermediate/",
  output_dir = "../../../path/to/even/deeper/output/",
  clean=FALSE)
```

But that's a bit unusual.

title: Support `opts_template`
description:
The new `opts_template` options are not supported in the existing `knitr_options`.  These can be set in the same way the other options can be set, using `$set()` and `$get()`.

Currently any templates defined before calling `render` work as expected but it would be preferable to have explicit support.

title: Output Format-specific `output_file`
description:
I am currently using various knitr options with pandoc to render multiple distinct versions of an output file to different locations.  

To clarify, I have a top-level directory structure like:
- `src`
- `build`
- `data`

I currently place all knitr cache, knitr figures, build markdown and pdf/html output in the `build` directory.  This makes it easier to identify generated artifacts from the source files, as well as keep multiple output (from multiple knit/pandoc calls) files separate.

It would be great if I could transition this process over to `render` using different  `output_format`s and use the Rstudio UI.  However, it seems that both the intermediate and output files are defined inside `render` based on the filename when no `output_file` argument is defined (as happens from the rstudio UI).  This means that I'd need to use a post-processor to move the initial output file to my target location, populating my source directory with ambiguous output.

Maybe `output_format` could return a filename to render so that `output_format`s could choose their `output_file`s?

- a vignette from package X has been written in R Markdown
- you look at the vignette in the Viewer pane

then the LaTeX math is very small.

It seems that all four of the above conditions are required in order to get the small math.

Now that I'm using R Markdown for package vignettes, I wonder if there is some trick I should be employing to keep it from happening.

title: Handle index.html
description:
When `run`ning with a NULL `file` and a given directory, we should serve up an `index.html` file if it's available and an `index.Rmd` file is not when a user visits the root path. This matters for Shiny Server, etc.

It turns out that doing this in the current architecture is not feasible without the ability to setup custom routes in Shiny being exported. Returning HTML directly from the UI gets us close, but still has all of the shiny.js/css in the `<head>` and just embeds whatever HTML you return inside of a `<body>`, which is probably not the expected behavior for an `index.html` file.

Might involve changes in Shiny and/or belong in that repo, but marking it here so it's recorded somewhere.

title: Cannot call `render` in a code chunk of the file being rendered
description:
Running `rmarkdown::render` on an Rmd document that contains a code chunk that calls `render` on a different file throws the following error:

```
Error in env$metadata <- list() :
  cannot change value of locked binding for 'metadata'
```

It appears to be thrown in [render.R](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/master/R/render.R#L245) during the exit cleanup. The nested call resets the binding to "metadata" and locks `render`'s environment, and when the outer call tries to do the same, it fails because the environment is already locked.

title: pandoc_path_arg: documentation and code are inconsistent
description:
The documentation says that pandoc_path_arg converts all backslashes to forward slashes under Windows, but the code converts all forward slashes to backslashes:

```
path <- gsub('/', '\\\\', path)
```

I am not submitting a pull-request because it is not clear what the desired behavior is: Is the error in the documentation or the code? Either way, the two should be consistent.

My sense is that the behavior described in the documentation is preferable: If there are backslashes in  a pandoc_path_arg, then template-substitutions can run into trouble with the ambiguity whether a backslash is a path separator or signals an escape sequence.

title: Feature request: output `beamer_presentation` with option for `latex_engine`
description:
knitr works with pdflatex as default, but for CJK scripts etc. xelatex or lualatex is necessary. For the time being, this can be invoked by adding a pandoc option like this: 

```
output: 
  beamer_presentation:
    pandoc_args: '--latex-engine=xelatex'
```

but an option for direct support in Rmarkdown should be easier to write: 

```
latex_engine: xelatex
```

Same for lualatex. 

Thanks for listening.

title: Default HTML template is not HTML5-compliant
description:
I received an email from CRAN because I put an HTML file generated by rmarkdown inside a package. Apparently they now run those HTML files through the W3C HTML5 validator at http://validator.w3.org/.

This is the error:

```
/data/rsync/PKGS/R6/inst/doc/Performance.html:
  Valid: FALSE (errors: 2, warnings: 2)
  Errors:
    line  col  message
       9   59  Bad value Content-Style-Type for attribute http-equiv on element meta.
     478   56  Consecutive hyphens did not terminate a comment. -- is not permitted inside a comment, but e.g. - - is.
```

These are in the template at: 
https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/f4a462fe7c47f3acbae71bfc6ae3597c15dd5c36/inst/rmd/h/default.html#L9
https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/f4a462fe7c47f3acbae71bfc6ae3597c15dd5c36/inst/rmd/h/default.html#L134

For the first error: in HTML5, the `http-equiv="Content-Style-Type"` is unknown:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6320084/why-is-meta-http-equiv-content-script-type-mostly-unused

For the second error, the problem is the `--self-contained` inside the `<!-- ... -->` tag.

In the future, as people start using rmarkdown for vignettes, they'll start running into this problem when they send packages to CRAN.

title: pandoc errors from render() when intermediates_dir and output_dir != input dir
description:
Using `rmarkdown_0.2.46`.

Re: `render()`

I find that it is very brittle when setting `intermediates_dir` and `output_dir` to values other than the directory of the input source.

Specifically, almost any setting for `intermediates_dir` causes pandoc to give a fatal error about not being able find a file it needs.

Also, if sending intermediate files and html files to the same, non-source directory, I get similar errors, unless there's a happy coincidence re: where that directory is in the hierarchy.

I made a small repository that reproduces the errors:
https://github.com/jennybc/arms-length-render

and the `README.md` gives the beginnings of a diagnosis and fix.

This comes up in projects with nontrivial directory structure and where you want to save intermediate Markdown, due to the benefits on GitHub. I use a generic `.rmd` file to process many input datasets. I do this via a wrapper script that takes the data file as a command line argument and programmatically constructs the path and filenames for the intermediates and outputs.

One last thing re: intermediate files. When `clean = FALSE` in `render()`, `foo.rmd` leads to `foo.knit.md` and then `foo.utf.md`. This is kind of unfortunate for the GitHub workflow where the intermediate Markdown is precious. I'd much prefer to be left with a file named just `foo.md`.

title: Support for multiple output types of the same generic format?
description:
The current structure of the render function assumes that while a user may want to generate multiple different outputs from the same source, that user would only want one `html_document`, one `pdf_document`, etc.  

Having used this same workflow for some time (via pandoc and Make), I find that I often want multiple outputs of the same type. For instance, I may have one `pdf_document` in which the pandoc options are configured the way a journal insists upon for preprints and another to actually look pretty.  Hacking out my own [custom format](http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/developer_custom_formats.html) seems rather silly when all I want is something with, say, two different templates like this:

``` yaml
output:
  pdf_document:
    template: pretty_template.tex

  pdf_document_for_review:
    keep_tex: true
    template: stupid_1990s_compatible_template.tex
```

Would it be reasonable to support multiple output formats of the same type by separating the name of the desired output (e.g. `pdf_document`) from the definition? Perhaps something like:

``` yaml
output:
  my_custom_output:
    format: pdf_document
    ...
```

title: The environment for rmarkdown::run()
description:
Because the `render_args` argument of `run()` is NULL, the default environment for R code chunks is the parent frame of an internal function (perhaps `shiny::maskReactiveContext`). This can cause confusion when `source()` is used in an R code chunk: http://stackoverflow.com/q/23880848/559676

``````

---
title: "Untitled"
runtime: shiny
output: html_document

---

Test.

```{r test}
environment()
## <environment: 0x46b11d0>
```
``````

We can blame `source()` on its bad default argument value (I think `local = TRUE` should be the default), but I guess perhaps the `render_args` argument can pass the parent environment of `run()` to `render()`, e.g. `render_args = list(envir = parent.frame())`. This does not solve the problem completely (the root problem is still `source(local = FALSE)`), but in most cases, `parent.frame()` is `globalenv()`, so we can at least cure the symptom although the illness is still there.

title: Set knitr figure device `dev` by output type?

For instance, I usually want this to `pdf` in pdf/latex outputs but `svg` or `png` in html outputs. Before `rmarkdown` I've always relied on writing a custom script to set these chunk options before calling `knit`, but it would be more tidy to have this in the header.  

Thanks for considering!

title: run(dir="...") Fails if Working Dir has an "index.Rmd" in it
description:
@jmcphers ,

(This is on the `feature/shiny-dependencies` branch).

I'm continuing to encounter some weirdness around the dir/file args in run(). I'm realizing that the PR I sent yesterday was indeed a partial fix for one of the issues, but didn't fix them all. I looked over the code as you have it now and didn't see an obvious fix so I thought I'd run it by you.

Part of the issue I believe is here: https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/blob/feature/shiny-dependencies/R/shiny.R#L69 . There, we're checking for a file named `index.Rmd` (by default) not in the location specified by `dir`, but in the current directory -- creating errors like:

```
Error in run(dir = "/home/shiny/ShinyApps/rmd") : 
  The file '/home/shiny/index.Rmd' does not exist in the directory '/home/shiny/ShinyApps/rmd'
```

(where `/home/shiny` is the working directory.) Often when the working directory does _not_ have an index.html file, I'll get an error or warning about the file not existing.

My PR doesn't do much better in this environment, unfortunately:

```
Error in run(dir = "/home/shiny/ShinyApps/rmd") : 
  The file '/home/shiny/ShinyApps/rmd//home/shiny/index.Rmd' does not exist
```

The path is absolute to help with detecting whether or not the file exists, but doesn't `join` cleanly onto the `dir` argument.

#

- Now remove a section and save; add the section back and save. Presentation might not be showing the Shiny outputs anymore. 

Note: In the following example, the ``` are escaped for inclusion in the ticket; they should be adjusted.

``````

---
title: "Shiny Document"
output: ioslides_presentation
runtime: shiny

---
## Title

This R Markdown document is made interactive using Shiny (for more information on Shiny see <http://shiny.rstudio.com>). Note that R Markdown documents using Shiny can currently only be run locally (support for running them within Shiny Server will be available soon).

## Table

You can embed Shiny inputs and outputs in your document. Outputs are automatically updated whenever inputs change. In this example we create a `numericInput` with the name "rows" and then refer to it's value via `input$rows` when generating output:

\```{r, echo=FALSE}
numericInput("rows", "How many cars?", 5)

renderTable({
  head(cars, input$rows)
})
\```

## Plot

In this example the output code was wrapped in a call to `renderTable`. There are many other render functions in Shiny that can be used for plots, printed R output, and more. This example uses `renderPlot` to create dynamic plot output:

\```{r, echo=FALSE}
sliderInput("bins", "Number of bins:", min = 1, max = 50, value = 30)

renderPlot({
  x <- faithful[, 2]  # Old Faithful Geyser data
  bins <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = input$bins + 1)

  # draw the histogram with the specified number of bins
  hist(x, breaks = bins, col = 'darkgray', border = 'white')
})
\```
``````

title: render() (really pandoc) can hang under certain circumstances
description:
This is _not a bug in rmarkdown_.  I report it here because it manifests itself by hanging rmarkdown::render() so there should be a  record of what is really going on.

render() tries to establish the version of pandoc available.   During this process  'pandoc --version' can hang forever (while using up all available memory) which causes render() to also hang forever.

I noticed this when trying to run render() in an ESS session running R on a remote server using tramp mode.   The environment on the remote ubuntu system apparently sets LC_ALL=C as part of it's localization.   As far as I can tell, on a ubuntu machine if the LC_ALL environment variable is set (to anything at all), the statically linked version of pandoc will hang.

This situation sounds exactly like ​(this bug)[https://ghc.haskell.org/trac/ghc/ticket/7344] reported 17 months ago.

Symptoms are 'pandoc --version' hangs and consumes memory until the process eventually dies with an OOM error. This seems to only happen when LC_ALL is set in the environment, and only when running the statically linked pandoc.

```
$ uname -a

$ wget https://s3.amazonaws.com/rstudio-buildtools/pandoc-1.12.3.zip

$ unzip pandoc-1.12.3.zip

title: Options set in a document function should not permanently set the global option state.
description:
Simple reproducible example, the key change here is setting the upload.fun option, this setting should not persist across render calls.

``` s
simple_html_format <- function() {
  require(rmarkdown)
    output_format(knitr = knitr_options(opts_knit = list(upload.fun= knitr::image_uri),
                                        opts_chunk = list(dev = 'png')),
        pandoc = pandoc_options(to = "html"))
}
#works fine
render('../vignettes/cars.Rmd', pdf_document())
#also works fine, but sets an option which breaks pdf_document
render('../vignettes/cars.Rmd', simple_html_format())
#breaks
render('../vignettes/cars.Rmd', pdf_document())
```

You can get the last render to work if you `opts_knit$restore()` after the simple_html_format call

I think the proper fix for this is to save all the option states before running a render, then restoring them after.

title: unable to render document a second time with custom cache.path
description:
The render function sets the fig.path function so that all figures end up in a predictable directory (e.g. for rendering "input.Rmd" to HTML it would be "input_files/figure_html"). This is for two reasons:
1. So that for non self-contained HTML dependent files end up in a single directory that can be easily transported along with the base page.
2. So that each distinct output format rendered has it's own figure directory (since they often have different default sizes).

For self_contained HTML the render function also removes the "input_files" directory after rendering (to leave a clean directory). Unfortunately if caching is enabled this results in the cached figures disappearing from underneath the cache! Therefore, render also sets the cache.path to e.g. "input_cache" and then preserves "input_files" if the cache was written to.

This is problematic in the case where the user sets a custom cache directory within their Rmd file. In this case render is unable to detect that a cache was used and goes ahead and deletes the "input_files/figure-html" directory (thus messing up the cache and making the next render fail).

What we really need is the ability for render to call knit and then after the fact detect whether any cached output was written (and in that case preserve input_files). 

@yihui Is there a knir hook we could write that would reliably detect whether any cached output was created or referenced during a knit?

title: Loading rmarkdown fails when installed knitr predates its xfun::attr() removal
description:
### Description

`renv::restore()` fails to install/load `rmarkdown` when the resolved dependency set pairs `xfun >= 0.56` with `knitr < 1.50`:

```
Error: object 'attr' is not exported by 'namespace:xfun'
Execution halted
Error: error testing if 'rmarkdown' can be loaded [error code 1]
```

### Root cause

- `knitr`'s `NAMESPACE` contained `importFrom(xfun, attr)` through knitr **1.49**. This was removed in knitr **1.50** (no longer imports `xfun::attr`).
- `xfun::attr()` was deprecated in xfun **0.52** and removed entirely in **0.56** (in favor of `xfun::attr2()`).
- rmarkdown's own source doesn't call `xfun::attr()` directly, but `DESCRIPTION` only requires `knitr (>= 1.43)` and `xfun (>= 0.36)`:

```
Imports: ... knitr (>= 1.43), ... xfun (>= 0.36), ...
```

Those floors independently satisfy renv/`install.packages()`, but together they allow an incompatible combination: any `knitr` in `[1.43, 1.50)` paired with any `xfun >= 0.56` breaks at namespace-load time, because loading `rmarkdown` loads `knitr`, which tries to import a symbol that no longer exists in `xfun`.

### Reproduction

With a lockfile pinning `knitr` to something `< 1.50` (e.g. `1.44`) and `xfun >= 0.56` (e.g. `0.60`), run `renv::restore()` — installing `rmarkdown` fails while renv tests whether the package can be loaded, since that transitively loads `knitr`.

### Suggested fix

Bump the `knitr` floor in `DESCRIPTION` to `knitr (>= 1.50)`, so `install.packages()`/renv can no longer resolve a `knitr`+`xfun` pair that's known to be incompatible.

### Environment

- R 4.3.1
- Encountered via `renv::restore()` in a CI/Jenkins backfill job after bumping `xfun` to 0.60 in `renv.lock`
- `rmarkdown` 2.31, `knitr` 1.44 (pre-fix), `xfun` 0.60 in the failing lockfile
